title: Data Science for Population Health Sciences
text:
Welcome
Population health research often begins with several imperfect files: a participant roster, a survey export, a table of clinic characteristics, or a record of study visits. Turning those files into a useful dataset requires decisions about what each row represents, how variables are recorded, and which records belong together.
Data Science for Population Health Sciences is a collection of practical, annotated R walkthroughs. Each chapter introduces a task, explains the decisions behind the code, and checks the result before moving to the next step. The aim is to help you understand and adapt a workflow to your own research.

title: Data Science for Population Health Sciences
text:
Start here
The first chapter, Data Preparation and Data Engineering, follows a fictional community-health study from raw CSV files to a participant dataset. It introduces basic cleaning, queries with dplyr and SQL through sqldf, six kinds of joins, and checks that help prevent accidental changes to your study sample.
The second part, Survey-Weighted Analysis with BRFSS 2024, applies the same habits to a national survey: the 2024 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS). It asks whether household income is associated with diabetes among adults in the participating jurisdictions and walks through importing the data, stacking questionnaire versions and joining a lookup table, cleaning, survey-weighted descriptive statistics, multiple imputation, and bivariate and multivariable survey-weighted regression. BRFSS data are public; you download them from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) yourself, and they stay on your computer.
In the first chapter, all example records are invented for teaching. They do not describe actual participants, clinics, or population health findings. The small files are included with the book so you can inspect every record and run the examples without downloading a research dataset.

section: How to work through a chapter
text:
How to work through a chapter

Read the question and predict what the next code block will do.
Run the code in order, starting with setup and data import.
Compare your output with the displayed result and its interpretation.
Try the practice questions before opening the suggested answers.

You should be comfortable opening R or RStudio and running a few lines of R. No SQL experience is assumed. The first chapter explains assignment, pipes, package-qualified function names, and common data types as they appear.
The contents menu takes you between chapters; the page outline takes you to a specific step. Sections start expanded, and you can collapse their panels or individual code blocks. Examples with two languages use dplyr and SQL tabs. Both tabs execute when the book is rendered.

title: Data Science for Population Health Sciences
text:
Run the book locally
Open pophealth-datascience.Rproj in RStudio, or open a terminal in the book’s root folder. Install R and Quarto, then restore the project’s R packages with renv::restore() as shown in the first chapter. Then run:
quarto preview
To create the complete HTML book without starting a preview server:
quarto render
Open _book/index.html after rendering. All chapter paths are relative to the book’s root folder, where _quarto.yml is located. Each chapter keeps its own analysis code together and should be run from its beginning in a fresh R session.
The survey chapters need the BRFSS files (see the first survey chapter) and several gigabytes of memory. To work on the first chapter alone, render it by itself:
quarto render chapters/data-preparation.qmd

title: 1  Data Preparation and Data Engineering
text:
NoteThe task: build a participant dataset





Imagine that you are preparing data for a community-health study. You receive three files: a participant roster, a clinic lookup table, and a study-visit extract. Before describing the participants, you need to clean the roster, connect the files, and confirm that the result still has the intended rows.
Data cleaning makes values interpretable and consistent. Data engineering organizes and connects data so those values can be used reliably. In this chapter, the final dataset will contain one row per enrolled participant, with clinic information and counts of records in the visit extract.
By the end of the walkthrough, you will be able to:

Import CSV files while preserving identifiers and raw values.
Inspect types, duplicates, missingness, and implausible entries.
Rename, recode, and derive variables with readable R code.
Select, filter, sort, and summarize data using both dplyr and SQL.
Explain and use left, inner, right, full, semi, and anti joins.
Check the unit of observation before and after joining tables.
Save a prepared dataset and a short record of what changed.

The files are small and entirely fictional. We will prepare data and produce descriptive summaries; these are not findings about a real population.






Figure 1.1: A workflow from preserved raw files through inspection, cleaning, queries and joins, validation, and new derived outputs.

1.2 Step 1: Set up the workspace






NotePackages, paths, and a few R conventions





Open the project’s .Rproj file to activate renv, then restore the recorded packages in your R console before rendering the book. The lockfile records R 4.6.2; install R and Quarto separately. This displayed command does not run during rendering:
renv::restore()
dplyr transforms data; sqldf runs SQL queries on R data frames; knitr formats tables; and rmarkdown supports Quarto’s R execution. We use base R to read and write CSV files. Quarto itself is installed separately.
Open the supplied .Rproj file, or start R in the folder containing _quarto.yml. During rendering, execute-dir: project makes paths resolve from that folder. For example, data/raw/participants.csv means a file inside this book, not a location elsewhere on your computer.


Show / hide code
options(width = 80)

# Keep SQL examples on the same database engine throughout the chapter.
options(sqldf.driver = "SQLite")

# Use sqldf's R-based string processing without a Tcl/Tk display dependency.
options(gsubfn.engine = "R")


You will see a few conventions throughout:







Notation
Meaning




participants <- ...
Save a result in an object named participants.


dplyr::filter()
Use filter() from the dplyr package. No library() call is needed.


data |> function()
Pass the data on the left into the next function. Read it as “then.”


# ...
A comment explaining the code or a decision.


NA
A missing value in R. It is different from zero or the text "NA".


==
Test equality. Use <- to assign an object.



Run the R chunks from top to bottom. Later examples use objects created earlier.

1.3 Step 2: Import and understand the files






NoteBegin with the row, the key, and the codebook





Download or inspect the participant roster, clinic table, and visit extract. Their complete codebook describes the invented values and deliberate data problems.
A key is a column, or combination of columns, used to identify or connect records. Before joining anything, state what one row represents:









File
Intended unit of observation
Key
Connection




Participants
One person
Participant ID
Each person belongs to one clinic.


Clinics
One clinic
clinic_id
A clinic can have several participants.


Visits
One recorded visit
visit_id
A participant can have several visits.



For these small teaching files, import every column as text first. That preserves IDs such as "001" and lets us inspect the recorded values before converting numeric and date columns. With a larger file, you can instead specify a type for each column.


Show / hide code
participants_raw <- read.csv(
  "data/raw/participants.csv",
  colClasses = "character",
  na.strings = c("", "NA"),
  check.names = FALSE
)

clinics <- read.csv(
  "data/raw/clinics.csv",
  colClasses = "character",
  na.strings = c("", "NA")
)

visits_raw <- read.csv(
  "data/raw/visits.csv",
  colClasses = "character",
  na.strings = c("", "NA")
)

1.4 Step 3: Clean the participant roster

1.4.1 Give variables readable names






NoteCreate a working copy





Use names that are easy to type and explain. rename() uses new_name = old_name. Backticks let R refer to an existing name that contains spaces. Assign the result to a new object so the imported source remains available for comparison.


Show / hide code
participants_named <- participants_raw |>
  dplyr::rename(
    participant_id = `Participant ID`,
    clinic_id = Clinic,
    age = Age,
    smoking = Smoking,
    enrollment_date = `Enrollment Date`,
    activity_minutes = `Activity Minutes`
  )

names(participants_named)


[1] "participant_id"   "clinic_id"        "age"              "smoking"         
[5] "enrollment_date"  "activity_minutes"







1.4.2 Inspect duplicates before removing them






NoteAn identical row is different from a repeated ID





First inspect all rows belonging to repeated participant IDs.


Show / hide code
duplicate_ids <- participants_named |>
  dplyr::count(participant_id, name = "n_rows") |>
  dplyr::filter(n_rows > 1)

participants_named |>
  dplyr::filter(participant_id %in% duplicate_ids$participant_id)


  participant_id clinic_id age smoking enrollment_date activity_minutes
1            002       C01  52      No      2026-01-06               60
2            002       C01  52      No      2026-01-06               60


Show / hide code
sum(duplicated(participants_named))


[1] 1


Participant 002 appears twice with exactly the same values. In the fictional source documentation, the second row is a confirmed duplicate export row. We can therefore remove the repeated whole row with distinct().


Show / hide code
participants_unique <- participants_named |>
  dplyr::distinct()

data.frame(
  rows_before = nrow(participants_named),
  rows_after = nrow(participants_unique),
  duplicate_rows_removed = nrow(participants_named) - nrow(participants_unique)
)


  rows_before rows_after duplicate_rows_removed
1          13         12                      1


We now have 12 rows. Do not use distinct(participant_id, .keep_all = TRUE) to resolve conflicting records without a reason: it keeps the first row and can silently discard information. Repeated IDs in a visit table, on the other hand, may represent valid visits.





1.4.3 Standardize text and convert types






NoteMake representation consistent before recoding





trimws() removes surrounding spaces; tolower() makes capitalization consistent. Neither function decides what a response means.


Show / hide code
participants_text <- participants_unique |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    participant_id = trimws(participant_id),
    clinic_id = trimws(clinic_id),
    smoking = tolower(trimws(smoking))
  )

table(participants_text$smoking, useNA = "ifany")



      n      no refused unknown       y     yes 
      2       4       1       1       1       3 


Next convert age and activity to numbers and enrollment dates to R’s Date type. Check the format rather than letting ambiguous dates be guessed.


Show / hide code
participants_typed <- participants_text |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    age = as.numeric(age),
    activity_minutes = as.numeric(activity_minutes),
    enrollment_date = as.Date(enrollment_date, format = "%Y-%m-%d")
  )

str(participants_typed)


'data.frame':   12 obs. of  6 variables:
 $ participant_id  : chr  "001" "002" "003" "004" ...
 $ clinic_id       : chr  "C01" "C01" "C02" "C02" ...
 $ age             : num  34 52 29 999 45 61 38 24 70 33 ...
 $ smoking         : chr  "yes" "no" "n" "unknown" ...
 $ enrollment_date : Date, format: "2026-01-05" "2026-01-06" ...
 $ activity_minutes: num  120 60 180 90 -9 0 NA 210 -20 150 ...


Show / hide code
# Converting valid recorded values should not introduce new missing values.
conversion_check <- data.frame(
  variable = c("age", "activity_minutes", "enrollment_date"),
  missing_before = c(
    sum(is.na(participants_text$age)),
    sum(is.na(participants_text$activity_minutes)),
    sum(is.na(participants_text$enrollment_date))
  ),
  missing_after = c(
    sum(is.na(participants_typed$age)),
    sum(is.na(participants_typed$activity_minutes)),
    sum(is.na(participants_typed$enrollment_date))
  )
)

stopifnot(conversion_check$missing_before == conversion_check$missing_after)


stopifnot() stops execution if an expected condition is false. Here it checks for failed conversions. If this fails on your own data, inspect the original values and confirm their format; do not just suppress a conversion warning. This check does not prove that the original dates were recorded correctly.





1.4.4 Use the codebook to interpret missing and invalid values






NoteMissing is not zero, and an invalid entry needs review





The codebook defines age 999 and activity -9 as not reported. These meanings come from this example’s documentation, not from the numbers themselves. Recode only those known sentinel values first.


Show / hide code
participants_missing <- participants_typed |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    age = dplyr::na_if(age, 999),
    activity_minutes = dplyr::na_if(activity_minutes, -9)
  )


Check against the fictional study’s documented range rules: ages 18–100 and activity between 0 and the total minutes in seven days. Flag a value before changing it, so the reason is visible.


Show / hide code
participants_flagged <- participants_missing |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    age_invalid = !is.na(age) & (age < 18 | age > 100),
    activity_invalid = !is.na(activity_minutes) &
      (activity_minutes < 0 | activity_minutes > 7 * 24 * 60)
  )

participants_flagged |>
  dplyr::filter(age_invalid | activity_invalid) |>
  dplyr::select(participant_id, age, activity_minutes, activity_invalid)


  participant_id age activity_minutes activity_invalid
1            009  70              -20             TRUE


Participant 009 has an unresolved activity value of −20. We cannot infer the correct value. For this example, preserve the flag and raw file, and set the cleaned value to missing. No participant is removed because of missing data.
We also combine documented variants of yes/no. Unknown and refused responses remain missing; they are not “No.” The raw response is still in participants_raw if we need to distinguish reasons for missingness later.


Show / hide code
# Stop for a new, undocumented category instead of silently recoding it.
stopifnot(
  all(is.na(participants_flagged$smoking) |
        participants_flagged$smoking %in%
          c("yes", "y", "no", "n", "unknown", "refused"))
)

participants_clean <- participants_flagged |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    age = dplyr::if_else(age_invalid, NA_real_, age),
    activity_minutes = dplyr::if_else(
      activity_invalid, NA_real_, activity_minutes
    ),
    smoking = dplyr::case_when(
      smoking %in% c("yes", "y") ~ "Yes",
      smoking %in% c("no", "n") ~ "No",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    age_group = dplyr::case_when(
      is.na(age) ~ NA_character_,
      age < 40 ~ "18-39",
      age < 60 ~ "40-59",
      TRUE ~ "60-100"
    ),
    age_group = factor(age_group, levels = c("18-39", "40-59", "60-100"))
  )

table(participants_clean$smoking, useNA = "always")



  No  Yes <NA> 
   6    4    2 


Show / hide code
table(participants_clean$age_group, useNA = "always")



 18-39  40-59 60-100   <NA> 
     5      4      2      1 


Show / hide code
colSums(is.na(participants_clean))


  participant_id        clinic_id              age          smoking 
               0                0                1                2 
 enrollment_date activity_minutes      age_invalid activity_invalid 
               0                3                0                0 
       age_group 
               1 


case_when() evaluates conditions from top to bottom; ~ separates a condition from its replacement. NA_real_ and NA_character_ explicitly create numeric and text missing values. A factor stores categories with specified levels, so age groups display in the intended order. These age cutpoints are teaching choices, not a required categorization for another analysis.
The cleaned roster has 1 missing age, 2 missing smoking responses, and 3 missing activity values. Participant 006’s reported zero activity minutes remains zero.
Finally, verify that participant IDs are present and unique after cleaning.


Show / hide code
stopifnot(
  !anyNA(participants_clean$participant_id),
  all(participants_clean$participant_id != ""),
  anyDuplicated(participants_clean$participant_id) == 0
)

1.5 Step 4: Ask questions with dplyr and SQL






NoteTwo ways to express the same operation





SQL stands for Structured Query Language. With sqldf::sqldf(), you write a SQL query inside an R string. The function copies the referenced R data frames into a temporary database, executes the query, and returns a new data frame. No database server is needed for this walkthrough. See the sqldf documentation.
We use SQLite explicitly. SQL syntax differs somewhat between database engines. The right and full joins later in the chapter require SQLite 3.39 or later. Check the version bundled with your installed RSQLite package:


Show / hide code
sqlite_version <- sqldf::sqldf("SELECT sqlite_version() AS version")
sqlite_version


  version
1  3.52.0


If it is older than 3.39, update RSQLite in the R console and restart R. SQLite added right and full outer joins in its 3.39 release.
For the initial queries, use only simple text and numeric columns. Dates and factors have special R classes; their behavior across database engines deserves separate attention when you move beyond these examples.


Show / hide code
people <- participants_clean |>
  dplyr::select(participant_id, clinic_id, age, smoking, activity_minutes)

1.5.4 Summarize by clinic






NoteCount people and observed values separately





Compute each clinic’s participant count, the number reporting activity, and the mean among those observed values. Keep groups with at least three participants.

dplyrSQL

activity_dplyr <- people |>
  dplyr::group_by(clinic_id) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_participants = dplyr::n(),
    n_activity_observed = sum(!is.na(activity_minutes)),
    mean_activity = mean(activity_minutes, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(n_participants >= 3) |>
  dplyr::arrange(clinic_id)

If a group has no observed values, R returns NaN and SQLite returns NULL; neither represents a measured mean. See SQLite’s aggregate-function documentation.
Each clinic has four participants, but the activity means use different denominators. These summaries describe the fictional records only. Ignoring missing values is not an imputation method or an assurance against bias.
WHERE filters individual records before grouping; HAVING filters groups after summarizing. .groups = "drop" makes the dplyr result ungrouped, so later operations do not silently continue within clinics.

text:
1.6 Step 5: See what different joins retain






NoteFollow actual rows through the join





A join connects two tables using matching keys. The left table is the first argument to a dplyr join, or the table after SQL’s FROM; the right table is the second argument, or the table after JOIN.
Start with two tiny tables so you can predict every output. These are separate teaching objects, not additional records in the study roster.


Show / hide code

  participant_id = c("001", "002", "003"),

The join produces 14 rows for 12 roster participants. Participants with two visits appear twice; those without a visit still appear once with missing visit fields. This table is useful for inspecting linked visits, but it no longer has one row per person. Averaging participant age across its rows would give more weight to people with more recorded visits.
If both tables repeat the same key, a many-to-many join can multiply rows further. Two rows for a person on one side and three on the other produce six matching combinations. Determine whether those combinations are intended before allowing that relationship. A cross join intentionally makes every pair of rows without a key; it is useful for tasks such as building a scheduling grid, but is not the participant-linkage operation we need here.
If the intended key is a combination, such as person and visit type, specify both: by = c("participant_id", "visit_type"). The SQL condition would use ON a.participant_id = b.participant_id AND a.visit_type = b.visit_type. Check uniqueness at that combined level; do not add a key merely to silence a join warning.

1.10 Before moving to an analysis






NoteQuestions to bring to your own dataset






What does one row represent in each file and in the final dataset?
Which keys should be unique, and are any keys missing?
Which cleaning rules came from documentation, and which remain unresolved?
Who was retained, who lacked a match, and did any join multiply rows?
What does a zero mean, and how does it differ from missing information?
Which denominator is used for each descriptive summary?
Can another analyst reproduce the prepared data from the preserved sources?

The next analysis can now begin with a documented participant dataset. Its missing-data strategy, eligibility criteria, and statistical model still need to follow the research question; successful data preparation does not determine those choices.

2.2 The Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System
The Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) is the largest continuously running health survey in the world. Every year, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the states interview hundreds of thousands of US adults by landline and cell phone about their health conditions, health behaviors, and use of health care. In 2024, 457,670 adults in 49 states, the District of Columbia, Guam, Puerto Rico, and the US Virgin Islands completed the interview (Tennessee did not collect enough data to be included).
The target is noninstitutionalized adults aged 18 or older in these participating jurisdictions. The combined results include the territories and exclude Tennessee; they are not estimates for all 50 states and DC. See the 2024 survey overview.
BRFSS is a complex survey:

Strata. Each state’s sample is drawn separately within strata (for example, by region and by landline or cell phone).
Primary sampling units (PSUs). Within a stratum, phone numbers are sampled. In BRFSS each respondent is their own PSU.
Weights. People are sampled with different probabilities and respond at different rates. CDC’s final weight (_LLCPWT) adjusts for selection and nonresponse and makes the weighted sample match each state’s adult population by age, sex, race and ethnicity, education, and other characteristics (“raking”).

Every estimate in these chapters uses all three. Chapter 5 shows what happens when they are ignored.

title: 3  Data Engineering: Stacking and Joining
text:
NoteTwo ways to combine data, for two different jobs





Survey analyses often need more than one file. Before writing any code, ask what the new file adds:

More people, with the same variables. Several questionnaire versions of the same survey, several survey years, or several sites. These files are stacked: their rows are placed one under the other with dplyr::bind_rows(), and their columns are lined up by name.
More variables, for the same people (or places). A table of state names and regions, area-level measures for each county, or a second instrument completed by the same respondents. These files are joined: their columns are added side by side with dplyr::left_join(), matching rows on a key.

Figure 3.1 shows the difference.






Figure 3.1: Stacking keeps the columns and adds rows; a left join keeps the rows and adds columns.



Using a join where a stack is needed is a common mistake. If two questionnaire versions are joined on an identifier that never matches (for example, a key built as paste(SEQNO, 1) in one file and paste(SEQNO, 2) in the other), a full join keeps every row but treats each shared column as a different variable, so the result has STATE.x, STATE.y, and so on. Stacking the files gives one STATE column.
The data-preparation chapter walks through all six kinds of joins with small tables (Figure 1.2). This chapter applies the three most common operations to BRFSS:

stacking the BRFSS questionnaire version files to analyze an optional module asked in different states on different versions;
a left join that adds state names and Census regions to every respondent;
an inner join, which keeps only the respondents whose state is in both tables, and why survey analyses rarely want that.

title: 3  Data Engineering: Stacking and Joining
text:
3.2 Stacking questionnaire versions

3.2.1 Why BRFSS has version files
Every state asks the BRFSS core questions. States can also add optional modules, such as the Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) module, and some states split their sample across up to three questionnaire versions so that they can ask more modules, each of a part of their sample. CDC therefore releases:

the main (combined) file, with every respondent, the core questions, and the modules a state asked on all of its versions, weighted with _LLCPWT;
one version file for each questionnaire version (LLCP24V1.XPT, LLCP24V2.XPT, and so on), with the respondents who received that version, the modules asked on it, and a weight for that version (for example, _LCPWTV1).

To analyze a module, you need the respondents from every state that asked it, and each state’s respondents must come from the file in which it asked the module. That means stacking the pieces, each with its own weight. CDC explains the rules, with worked examples, in Complex Sampling Weights and Preparing Module Data for Analysis, published with each year’s data on the CDC BRFSS annual data page. Read the version for your survey year before you start.


3.2.2 Download the version files (optional)
The rest of the book uses only the main file. To run this section, download the SAS transport files for questionnaire versions 1, 2 and 3 from the CDC BRFSS 2024 multiple-questionnaire page, unzip them, and save them in data/brfss/raw/ as LLCP24V1.XPT, LLCP24V2.XPT and LLCP24V3.XPT (as with the main file, remove the trailing space from each unzipped file name). If the files are not there, the code in this section is shown but not run.


Show / hide code
options(timeout = 600) # allow 10 minutes on a slow connection
for (version in 1:3) {
  zip_file <- file.path(raw_dir, paste0("LLCP24V", version, "_XPT.ZIP"))
  utils::download.file(
    paste0(
      "https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/annual_data/2024/files/LLCP24V",
      version,
      "_XPT.ZIP"
    ),
    destfile = zip_file,
    mode = "wb"
  )
  extracted <- utils::unzip(zip_file, exdir = raw_dir)
  file.rename(extracted, file.path(raw_dir, paste0("LLCP24V", version, ".XPT")))
  file.remove(zip_file)
}




3.2.3 Step 1: Read each file with the same column names
To stack files, their columns must have the same names. Three things differ between the BRFSS files and are fixed as each file is read:

Underscore names. _STATE, _STSTR, and _PSU need backticks in every line of code. Renaming them once (to STATE, STSTR, PSU) avoids that.
The weight. Each file has its own weight variable. Renaming each one to FINALWT lines the weights up in one column when the files are stacked.
The module. A module’s items are only in the files where it was asked. Reading with dplyr::any_of() takes the item when it is there, and the function adds an empty column when it is not.

Set module_item to one item from the module you want to analyze. The ACE item used here is an example: check the 2024 codebook for the item you need and its name.


Show / hide code
module_item <- "ACEDEPRS" # one item from your module (check the codebook)
version_weights <- c(
  main = "_LLCPWT",
  v1 = "_LCPWTV1",
  v2 = "_LCPWTV2",
  v3 = "_LCPWTV3"
)

read_version <- function(source) {
  path <- file.path(raw_dir, version_files[[source]])
  weight <- version_weights[[source]]
  # Check: the weight we expect is in this file (read only the column names).
  if (!weight %in% names(haven::read_xpt(path, n_max = 0))) {
    stop(weight, " is not in ", path, ". Check the codebook for this file.")
  }
  data <- haven::read_xpt(
    path,
    col_select = dplyr::any_of(c(
      "SEQNO",
      "_STATE",
      "_STSTR",
      "_PSU",
      weight,
      module_item
    ))
  ) |>
    dplyr::rename(
      STATE = `_STATE`,
      STSTR = `_STSTR`,
      PSU = `_PSU`,
      FINALWT = dplyr::all_of(weight)
    ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(source = source)
  if (!module_item %in% names(data)) {
    data[[module_item]] <- NA_real_ # module not in this file
  }
  return(data)
}

pieces <- purrr::map(names(version_files), read_version) |>
  purrr::set_names(names(version_files))

The rule for choosing the rows follows from the file structure:

A state with the module in the main file asked it of its whole sample. Take that state’s respondents from the main file only, with _LLCPWT.
Any other state asked the module on one or more versions. Take its respondents from each version file in which it asked the module, with that version’s weight.

A state must never be taken from the main file and a version file at the same time, because the version files hold the same people as the main file, and they would be counted twice.

  dplyr::pull(STATE)

  dplyr::pull(STATE)

stacked <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  pieces$main |> dplyr::filter(STATE %in% states_main),
  pieces$v1 |> dplyr::filter(STATE %in% states_v1),
  pieces$v2 |> dplyr::filter(STATE %in% states_v2),
  pieces$v3 |> dplyr::filter(STATE %in% states_v3)
)

# one version.

3.2.6 Step 4: Adjust the weights for states with more than one version
Each version’s weight makes that version’s respondents represent the whole adult population of the state. A state that asked the module on two versions is therefore represented twice, once by each version’s respondents. To count it once, multiply each version’s weights by that version’s share of the state’s stacked sample, so that the shares within each state add up to 1:
\[
\text{FINALWT\_ADJ} = \text{FINALWT} \times
\frac{n_\text{version in the state}}{n_\text{all versions in the state}}
\]
States that come from a single file have a share of 1, so their weights are unchanged. If the versions are of similar size, CDC’s guidance also allows a constant (0.5 for two versions, about 0.33 for three).
In 2024 no state asked the ACE module on more than one version, so every share below is 1 and the adjustment leaves the ACE weights unchanged: the table printed after the check is empty. The step is still part of the recipe, because other modules need it. For example, Michigan asked the Cognitive Decline module on versions 1 and 3, so a stacked Cognitive Decline file would take Michigan’s respondents from both versions, and their weights would be multiplied by each version’s share.


Show / hide code
stacked <- stacked |>
  dplyr::add_count(STATE, name = "n_state") |>
  dplyr::add_count(STATE, source, name = "n_version") |>
  dplyr::mutate(FINALWT_ADJ = FINALWT * n_version / n_state)

# Check: within every state, the version shares add up to 1.
shares <- stacked |>
  dplyr::distinct(STATE, source, n_version, n_state) |>
  dplyr::summarise(total_share = sum(n_version / n_state), .by = STATE)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(shares$total_share, rep(1, nrow(shares)))))
dplyr::filter(stacked, n_version < n_state) |>
  dplyr::distinct(STATE, source, n_version, n_state)


# A tibble: 0 × 4
# ℹ 4 variables: STATE <dbl>, source <chr>, n_version <int>, n_state <int>


Make the adjustment right after stacking, before you drop any rows for missing answers or select a subgroup, so that the shares describe each version’s full sample in the state.

The stacked data use the adjusted weight with the same strata and PSUs as before. nest = TRUE tells the survey package that PSU codes repeat across strata.


Show / hide code
stacked_design <- stacked |>
  srvyr::as_survey_design(
    ids = PSU,
    strata = STSTR,
    weights = FINALWT_ADJ,
    nest = TRUE
  )

3.3 Joining a lookup table
BRFSS stores each respondent’s state as a FIPS code (_STATE): 26 is Michigan and 39 is Ohio. A small lookup table, data/lookup/states.csv, gives each code a name, a postal abbreviation, and a US Census Bureau region. A left join adds those columns to every respondent and keeps every respondent, whether or not their code is in the lookup.

3.3.1 Step 1: Import the lookup table and check its key
The key is the column the join matches on. In the lookup, each code must appear exactly once; otherwise a respondent would match two rows and be duplicated (see the one-to-many example in the data-preparation chapter).


Show / hide code
states <- utils::read.csv(
  "data/lookup/states.csv",
  colClasses = c(
    fips = "numeric",
    state_name = "character",
    state_abbr = "character",
    census_region = "character"
  )
)
# Check: one row per FIPS code, and no blank keys.
stopifnot(!anyNA(states$fips), !anyDuplicated(states$fips))
nrow(states)

An anti join returns the rows of the first table that have no match in the second. Run it in both directions before joining.

# Respondents whose state code is not in the lookup: these would get blank names.
no_lookup <- dplyr::anti_join(
  brfss,
  states,
  by = dplyr::join_by(`_STATE` == fips)

  states,
  dplyr::distinct(brfss, `_STATE`),
  by = dplyr::join_by(fips == `_STATE`)

  dplyr::left_join(
    states,
    by = dplyr::join_by(`_STATE` == fips),
    relationship = "many-to-one"

# Check: the same respondents, and every one has a state name.

TipJoining area-level data



The same steps work for any table with one row per place: county poverty rates from the American Community Survey, state policy indicators, and so on. Check the key, look for unmatched codes in both directions, state the relationship, and confirm the row count afterwards. Survey weights describe people, not places, so the joined columns are analyzed as characteristics of each respondent’s state.

section: 3.4 Inner join: keep only matches in both tables
text:
3.4 Inner join: keep only matches in both tables
A left join keeps every respondent. An inner join keeps only the rows whose key is in both tables: a respondent whose state has no row in the second table is dropped, without a warning. Figure 3.2 shows the difference.






Figure 3.2: An inner join drops the respondent whose state is not in the second table; a left join keeps that respondent with a blank region.



Inner joins are common when a second table covers only some places. Suppose an area-level table, such as one built from the American Community Survey, has a row for each of the 50 states and the District of Columbia but none for the territories. Here we make such a table from the lookup.

3.4.1 Step 1: Make a table that covers fewer states


Show / hide code
states_50_dc <- states |>
  dplyr::filter(census_region != "US territory")
# Check: the 50 states and the District of Columbia.
stopifnot(nrow(states_50_dc) == 51)




3.4.2 Step 2: Join

dplyrSQL




Show / hide code
brfss_50_dc <- brfss |>
  dplyr::inner_join(
    states_50_dc,
    by = dplyr::join_by(`_STATE` == fips),
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  )
nrow(brfss)


[1] 457670


Show / hide code
nrow(brfss_50_dc)


[1] 450353






Show / hide code
inner_count_sql <- sqldf::sqldf(
  'SELECT COUNT(*) AS n
   FROM brfss AS b
   INNER JOIN states_50_dc AS s ON b."_STATE" = s.fips'
)
inner_count_sql


       n
1 450353







3.4.3 Step 3: Find out who was dropped
An inner join reports nothing about the rows it drops, so count them yourself. The anti join from Section 3.3 lists them.


Show / hide code
dropped <- dplyr::anti_join(
  brfss,
  states_50_dc,
  by = dplyr::join_by(`_STATE` == fips)
)
# Check: the dropped and kept respondents add up to everyone, and SQL agrees with dplyr.
stopifnot(
  nrow(dropped) + nrow(brfss_50_dc) == nrow(brfss),
  inner_count_sql$n == nrow(brfss_50_dc)
)
dropped |>
  dplyr::count(`_STATE`) |>
  dplyr::left_join(states, by = dplyr::join_by(`_STATE` == fips)) |>
  dplyr::select(`_STATE`, state_name, n)


# A tibble: 3 × 3
  `_STATE` state_name            n
     <dbl> <chr>             <int>
1       66 Guam               1660
2       72 Puerto Rico        4309
3       78 US Virgin Islands  1348


The inner join dropped the 7,317 respondents from the territories.






ImportantInner joins and survey weights



Dropping rows before the survey design is declared is a way of selecting a subgroup, and for survey data it is the wrong way. The design needs every respondent’s stratum and primary sampling unit to estimate standard errors correctly, even when an estimate is about a subgroup. Keep every respondent with a left join, declare the design, and then select the subgroup from the design object, as Section 5.5 does for respondents with a known income (for example, design |> dplyr::filter(census_region != "US territory")).
Dropping entire independently sampled strata can be a special case, but simply calling the joined result a new dataset does not fix its variance estimates. Subsetting the design is the safer general workflow.


The next chapters use brfss_joined, the result of the left join, so every respondent is kept.

3.6 Practice

In the stacking example, what would go wrong if Michigan were taken from both the main file and the version 1 file?
Why must the weights be adjusted before rows with a missing module answer are dropped?
You receive a county table with two rows for one county (an old and a new name). What would the relationship = "many-to-one" argument do, and how would you fix the lookup?
You inner-join a survey that records each respondent’s county to a county table, and the result has 20,000 fewer rows than the survey. What two checks would you run, and how would you then estimate a prevalence for the counties in the table?







TipSuggested answers






Michigan’s version 1 respondents are also in the main file, so they would be counted twice, and Michigan would represent about twice its adult population.
The shares should reflect each version’s full sample in the state. Dropping rows first makes the shares depend on who answered, which changes the weights in a way the survey design does not intend.
dplyr would stop with an error, because some respondents would match two lookup rows. Keep one row per county code in the lookup (for example, the current name) and check anyDuplicated() again before joining.
Run an anti join to see which county codes did not match and how many respondents have each, and check whether the codes are missing from the county table or stored differently (for example, as text with leading zeros). Then left-join instead, declare the survey design on all respondents, and filter the design to the counties in the table.

title: 4  Cleaning and Recoding
text:
4.1 Step 1: Declare what each item can be
Raw Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) answers are numeric codes. Cleaning turns them into labeled categories that R and readers understand. It is also where most analysis errors start: a code that slips through unrecoded (a 99 for “refused” read as an income group) or a missing value silently turned into “no” changes every result that follows.
This chapter follows four rules:
The values below come from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) BRFSS 2024 codebook. BRFSS uses common codes for non-answers in these items: 7 (or 77) for “Don’t know/Not sure”, 9 (or 99) for “Refused”, and a blank (NA in R) for “Not asked or missing”.
Show / hide code
# Possible values of each item in the BRFSS 2024 codebook. Blank (NA) means "not asked or
# missing".
item_values <- list(
  DIABETE4 = c(1:4, 7, 9), # 1 Yes; 2 Yes, but only during pregnancy; 3 No;
  # 4 No, prediabetes or borderline; 7 Don't know; 9 Refused
  GENHLTH = c(1:5, 7, 9), # 1 Excellent; 2 Very good; 3 Good; 4 Fair; 5 Poor;
  # 7 Don't know; 9 Refused
  MEDCOST1 = c(1, 2, 7, 9), # 1 Yes; 2 No; 7 Don't know; 9 Refused
  INCOME3 = c(1:11, 77, 99), # 1 Less than $10,000 ... 11 $200,000 or more;
  # 77 Don't know; 99 Refused
  `_AGE_G` = 1:6, # 1 18-24; 2 25-34; 3 35-44; 4 45-54; 5 55-64; 6 65+
  `_AGE80` = 18:80, # CDC-imputed age in years; 80 means 80 or older
  SEXVAR = 1:2, # 1 Male; 2 Female
  `_IMPRACE` = 1:6, # 1 White; 2 Black; 3 Asian; 4 American Indian or Alaska
  # Native (all non-Hispanic); 5 Hispanic; 6 Other, non-Hispanic
  EDUCA = c(1:6, 9), # 1 Never attended ... 6 College 4 years or more; 9 Refused
  EMPLOY1 = 1:9, # 1 Employed for wages ... 8 Unable to work; 9 Refused
  `_STATE` = c(1, 2, 4:6, 8:13, 15:42, 44:46, 48:51, 53:56, 66, 72, 78) # FIPS codes
)
# The design variables, the CDC-imputed items, and the state columns joined in
# the previous chapter are never blank.
never_blank <- c(
  "_LLCPWT",
  "_STSTR",
  "_PSU",
  "_STATE",
  "_AGE_G",
  "_AGE80",
  "SEXVAR",
  "_IMPRACE",
  "state_abbr",
  "census_region"
)
The 53 state codes are the 2024 codebook’s: the 50 states except Tennessee (47), plus the District of Columbia (11), Guam (66), Puerto Rico (72), and the US Virgin Islands (78).

4.2 Step 2: Check the data against the codebook
A codebook can be wrong, and a file can change between releases. This check compares every observed value with the declaration and stops, naming each item and value, if anything else appears. It is silent when the data are as declared.


Show / hide code
# Check: every value is in the codebook.
unexpected <- purrr::imap(item_values, \(values, item) {
  setdiff(brfss[[item]], c(values, NA))
}) |>
  purrr::compact()
if (length(unexpected) > 0) {
  stop(
    "Values not in the codebook: ",
    paste0(
      names(unexpected),
      " (",
      purrr::map_chr(unexpected, toString),
      ")",
      collapse = "; "
    )
  )
}
# Check: no blanks where the codebook has none, and every weight is positive.
stopifnot(!anyNA(brfss[never_blank]), all(brfss[["_LLCPWT"]] > 0))

title: 4  Cleaning and Recoding
text:
4.3 Step 3: Recode
dplyr::recode_values() maps each code (left of ~) to a value (right of ~). With unmatched = "error", any code we did not list stops the run, so nothing can slip through. tidylog::mutate() works like dplyr::mutate() but reports what each new variable looks like, including its share of missing values.
Four decisions are built into this recoding (Appendix A lists them with counts):

Non-answers become missing. “Don’t know”, “refused”, and blank do not supply a usable value, so they become NA. The reasons for missingness may still be informative. Chapter 6 fills in missing values under stated assumptions.
Define the outcome explicitly. A report of diabetes only during pregnancy (DIABETE4 = 2) is coded “No” for our outcome of reported diagnosed diabetes excluding pregnancy-only diabetes. This is a survey classification, not proof that the person has no diabetes now. Undiagnosed diabetes is not measured here.
Age and race and ethnicity come from CDC’s imputed versions. CDC fills the few missing answers for these weighting variables (_AGE_G, _IMPRACE), so they are never blank. Six age groups adjust for age much better than two.
Reference groups come first. The first level of each factor is the comparison group in the models: the lowest income group, ages 18-24, female, and non-Hispanic White (the largest group).



Show / hide code
brfss_clean <- brfss |>
  tidylog::mutate(
    diabetes = dplyr::recode_values(
      DIABETE4,
      1 ~ "Yes",
      c(2, 3) ~ "No", # pregnancy-only diabetes is excluded from this outcome
      4 ~ "Prediabetes",
      c(7, 9, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(levels = c("No", "Prediabetes", "Yes")),
    genhlth = dplyr::recode_values(
      GENHLTH,
      1 ~ "Excellent",
      2 ~ "Very good",
      3 ~ "Good",
      4 ~ "Fair",
      5 ~ "Poor",
      c(7, 9, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(levels = c("Excellent", "Very good", "Good", "Fair", "Poor")),
    cost_barrier = dplyr::recode_values(
      MEDCOST1,
      1 ~ "Yes",
      2 ~ "No",
      c(7, 9, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    income = dplyr::recode_values(
      INCOME3,
      1:4 ~ "Less than $25,000",
      5:6 ~ "$25,000 to $49,999",
      7:8 ~ "$50,000 to $99,999",
      9:11 ~ "$100,000 or more",
      c(77, 99, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(
        levels = c(
          "Less than $25,000",
          "$25,000 to $49,999",
          "$50,000 to $99,999",
          "$100,000 or more"
        )
      ),
    age_group = dplyr::recode_values(
      `_AGE_G`,
      1 ~ "18-24",
      2 ~ "25-34",
      3 ~ "35-44",
      4 ~ "45-54",
      5 ~ "55-64",
      6 ~ "65 or older",
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(
        levels = c("18-24", "25-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55-64", "65 or older")
      ),
    age = as.numeric(`_AGE80`),
    sex = dplyr::recode_values(
      SEXVAR,
      1 ~ "Male",
      2 ~ "Female",
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(levels = c("Female", "Male")),
    race_eth = dplyr::recode_values(
      `_IMPRACE`,
      1 ~ "Non-Hispanic White",
      2 ~ "Non-Hispanic Black",
      3 ~ "Non-Hispanic Asian",
      4 ~ "Non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native",
      5 ~ "Hispanic",
      6 ~ "Non-Hispanic other race",
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(
        levels = c(
          "Non-Hispanic White",
          "Non-Hispanic Black",
          "Non-Hispanic Asian",
          "Non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native",
          "Hispanic",
          "Non-Hispanic other race"
        )
      ),
    education = dplyr::recode_values(
      EDUCA,
      1:3 ~ "Less than high school",
      4 ~ "High school graduate",
      5 ~ "Some college",
      6 ~ "College graduate",
      c(9, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(
        levels = c(
          "Less than high school",
          "High school graduate",
          "Some college",
          "College graduate"
        )
      ),
    employment = dplyr::recode_values(
      EMPLOY1,
      1:2 ~ "Employed",
      3:4 ~ "Out of work",
      5:6 ~ "Homemaker or student",
      7 ~ "Retired",
      8 ~ "Unable to work",
      c(9, NA) ~ NA,
      unmatched = "error"
    ) |>
      factor(
        levels = c(
          "Employed",
          "Out of work",
          "Homemaker or student",
          "Retired",
          "Unable to work"
        )
      ),
    state = factor(state_abbr),
    region = factor(
      census_region,
      levels = c("Northeast", "Midwest", "South", "West", "US territory")
    ),
    # 0/1 outcomes for the models. `==` keeps missing values missing (`%in%` would not).
    diabetes_yes = as.integer(diabetes == "Yes"),
    fair_poor = as.integer(genhlth == "Fair" | genhlth == "Poor")
  ) |>
  # PSU codes repeat across strata: number each stratum-PSU pair.
  tidylog::mutate(psu_id = dplyr::cur_group_id(), .by = c(`_STSTR`, `_PSU`))

WarningA common trap with missing values



genhlth %in% c("Fair", "Poor") returns FALSE (not NA) when genhlth is missing, so everyone with a missing answer would be counted as being in good health. Comparisons with == keep missing values missing.








NoteWhy a new PSU identifier?



In BRFSS, primary sampling unit (PSU) codes are only unique within a stratum: PSU 1 in one stratum is a different phone number from PSU 1 in another. survey::svydesign() can combine them itself (nest = TRUE). Numbering each stratum-PSU pair once gives globally unique integer IDs and avoids repeated relabeling and a large nesting cross-tabulation. The speed difference depends on the installed survey backend; the weights, strata and clusters are unchanged. There are 457,670 pairs for 457,670 respondents: in BRFSS each respondent is their own PSU.

title: 4  Cleaning and Recoding
text:
4.4 Step 4: Check the recoding
The unmatched = "error" arguments already guarantee that every code was mapped. Five more checks confirm the rules we rely on later, including that every PSU identifier sits in a single stratum, which lets the survey designs in later chapters skip their own (slow) check of the same thing.


Show / hide code
# Check: the "only during pregnancy" answers are now "No", and the 0/1 outcomes are
# missing exactly where the outcomes are.
stopifnot(
  all(brfss_clean$diabetes[brfss_clean$DIABETE4 %in% 2] == "No"),
  identical(is.na(brfss_clean$diabetes_yes), is.na(brfss_clean$diabetes)),
  identical(is.na(brfss_clean$fair_poor), is.na(brfss_clean$genhlth))
)
# Check: every respondent has a Census region (a level we did not list would be NA).
stopifnot(!anyNA(brfss_clean$region))
# Check: each PSU identifier belongs to exactly one stratum (PSUs are nested in strata).
stopifnot(
  nrow(dplyr::distinct(brfss_clean, psu_id, `_STSTR`)) ==
    dplyr::n_distinct(brfss_clean$psu_id)
)

title: 5  Survey-Weighted Descriptive Statistics
text:
5.1 The survey design object
Descriptive statistics answer “what does the population look like?” With a complex survey such as the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS), every estimate has to use the survey design, or it describes the sample (who happened to answer the phone) rather than the target population in the participating jurisdictions. This chapter describes the observed data only: the answers people gave, with missing answers shown as missing. We use imputed values only for models in this book. Imputation can also support population descriptive estimates, but it does not describe which answers were observed.
The srvyr package lets us describe the design once and then use familiar dplyr verbs on it. The design object stores the data together with the three design features from Chapter 2:
Show / hide code
# Check again when reading a saved file: identifiers are nested and weights are valid.
stopifnot(
  !anyNA(brfss_clean[c("psu_id", "strata", "weight")]),
  all(is.finite(brfss_clean$weight)),
  all(brfss_clean$weight > 0),
  nrow(dplyr::distinct(brfss_clean, psu_id, strata)) ==
    dplyr::n_distinct(brfss_clean$psu_id)
)
design <- brfss_clean |>
  srvyr::as_survey_design(
    ids = psu_id,
    strata = strata,
    weights = weight,
    nest = FALSE,
    check_strata = FALSE
  )

title: 5  Survey-Weighted Descriptive Statistics
text:
ids: the primary sampling units (clusters);
strata: the strata;
weights: the final weight.








TipWhy check_strata = FALSE?



By default the design checks that every PSU lies within a single stratum. Depending on the survey package version, this check can create a large PSU-by-stratum table. The psu_id variable numbers each stratum-PSU pair, so the PSUs are nested in strata by construction. Chapter 4 verifies that each identifier belongs to exactly one stratum before this check is disabled. Keep the default check unless you have verified that nesting condition.









WarningWhat ignoring the design does




Without weights, estimates describe the sample, not the population. Groups that answer surveys more often (older adults, for example) count too much.
Without strata and clusters, standard errors are wrong, so confidence intervals and p-values are wrong too. Clustering usually makes them too small.




5.1.1 Strata with a single PSU
Variance estimation compares PSUs within each stratum, which is impossible when a stratum has only one PSU.


Show / hide code
brfss_clean |>
  tidylog::summarise(n_psu = dplyr::n_distinct(psu_id), .by = strata) |>

5.7.1 Weights change the estimate

5.7.2 The design changes the uncertainty
The design effect (DEFF) compares the variance of an estimate under the survey design with its variance under a simple random sample of the same size:
\[
\text{DEFF} = \frac{\text{Variance}_\text{survey design}}{\text{Variance}_\text{simple random sample}},
\qquad
n_\text{effective} = \frac{n}{\text{DEFF}}
\]
A DEFF of 2 means the survey gives as much information as a simple random sample half its size, and standard errors are \(\sqrt{2} \approx 1.4\) times larger.

  dplyr::summarise(
    diabetes = srvyr::survey_mean(diabetes_yes, na.rm = TRUE, deff = TRUE),
    n_diabetes = srvyr::unweighted(sum(!is.na(diabetes_yes))),
    fair_poor = srvyr::survey_mean(fair_poor, na.rm = TRUE, deff = TRUE),
    n_fair_poor = srvyr::unweighted(sum(!is.na(fair_poor)))
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    n_effective_diabetes = n_diabetes / diabetes_deff,

ImportantThree kinds of missing data




Missing completely at random (MCAR): missingness is unrelated to observed or missing data values. Dropping incomplete answers loses precision but does not bias estimates.
Missing at random (MAR): after conditioning on observed variables, missingness no longer depends on the missing values. Imputation can reduce bias if its models adequately represent the relevant relationships and survey design; MAR alone is not a guarantee.
Missing not at random (MNAR): missingness still depends on missing values after conditioning on observed variables (for example, people with very high incomes declining to say). Neither approach fixes this on its own; it calls for sensitivity analyses.

Income missingness varies with age and health, so MCAR is not plausible. Chapter 6 works under MAR. These observed patterns cannot distinguish MAR from MNAR.

title: 6  Multiple Imputation with Survey Data
text:
6.1 Why not just drop incomplete answers?
Most R modeling functions silently drop every respondent with a missing value in any model variable. Household income is missing for 19.1% of respondents, so a model of diabetes by income would lose about one adult in five. Chapter 5 showed that the people who do not report income differ in age and general health. Their weighted diabetes prevalence is similar to that of respondents who report income. Dropping them loses information and can bias the results.
Multiple imputation keeps everyone. It works in three steps:
We use the mice package (multivariate imputation by chained equations), which imputes one variable at a time from the others and cycles through them until the imputations stabilize.
crumbs: 6  Multiple Imputation with Survey Data

title: 6  Multiple Imputation with Survey Data
text:
Impute. Fill in each missing value with a plausible value drawn from a model that predicts it from everything else we know about the person. Do this several times (here, 5 times) to create 5 completed datasets. The imputed values differ between datasets, and that difference expresses our uncertainty about the true values.
Analyze. Fit the same model to each completed dataset (Chapter 7, Chapter 8).
Pool. Combine the 5 results with Rubin’s rules into one estimate and one standard error that includes the uncertainty from imputation.

section: 6.3 Making the imputation model reflect the survey design
text:
6.3 Making the imputation model reflect the survey design
Imputation models are regression models. If they ignore the survey design, the imputed values reflect the sample, and later weighted estimates can be biased. The practical recommendation is to represent relevant design features in the imputation model (Reiter, Raghunathan, and Kinney, 2006). This example makes a simplifying choice:

the weight is a predictor, so imputed values can vary with it;
the strata and primary sampling unit (PSU) identifiers stay untouched for the later survey analysis. A unique PSU for each person cannot provide a useful categorical predictor. Stratum effects can be modeled, but are omitted here;
the state can represent geographic differences, but its 53 categories add parameters to each imputation model. This teaching example omits state from the default predictor matrix. The example below shows how to include it when imputing income. For a substantive analysis, assess the consequences of this simplification rather than choosing predictors on computing time alone.
the Census region (Section 3.3) is a coarser summary of the same geography. It is also omitted here, so that the imputations match the worked example; try adding it as an exercise and compare.

Including the weight alone does not fully account for the sampling design. Treat the pooled results as a teaching illustration. A substantive analysis needs an assessment of geographic and stratum effects, suitable imputation models, and sensitivity to the missing-data assumptions.
The predictor matrix says which variables predict which: a 1 in row income, column weight means the weight is used to impute income.

6.4 How each variable is imputed
We impute every incomplete variable with predictive mean matching (PMM). For each person with a missing value, PMM predicts the value from a regression, finds the respondents with an observed value whose predictions are closest, and copies the observed value of one of them, chosen at random. Imputed values are therefore always real answers (an income group, never “2.4”). For factors, this version of mice derives a numerical score for matching and then copies the donor’s original category; it does not treat the category labels as measured quantities.

6.5 Imputing in parallel, reproducibly
Each completed dataset is independent of the others, so they can be imputed at the same time on different processor cores. furrr::future_map() runs one imputation per task, and mice::ibind() combines the single imputations into one object. future::plan() sets the number of parallel workers. First detect the available cores; reserve one core and use at most four workers, or fewer if there are fewer imputations. The cap limits memory use because each worker holds its own data.
The main example uses 5 imputations to keep a classroom run short. For a substantive analysis, assess the fraction of missing information and the stability of pooled estimates and standard errors, and increase the number of imputations when needed.
The seed argument makes the results reproducible. furrr gives each task its own random-number stream derived from the seed, independent of the number of workers. Reproducing the results also requires the same data, code, and software versions; numerical differences between platforms can still matter.

title: 7  Bivariate Survey-Weighted Regression
text:
7.1 Prevalence ratios
A bivariate (or “crude”, or “unadjusted”) model relates the outcome to one variable at a time. Crude associations describe the population; they are not causal effects, because other variables are not held constant. Chapter 8 adjusts for them.
Our outcome is reported diagnosed diabetes excluding pregnancy-only diabetes (1 = yes, 0 = no, prediabetes, or pregnancy-only diabetes). We compare its prevalence between groups with the prevalence ratio (PR), reported with its 95% confidence interval (CI):
\[
\text{PR} = \frac{\text{prevalence of diabetes in a group}}{\text{prevalence of diabetes in the reference group}}
\]
A PR of 2 means the group has twice the prevalence of the reference group. A Poisson regression with a log link and a 0/1 outcome estimates prevalence ratios directly (“modified Poisson” regression): its exponentiated coefficients are PRs. Two details:

title: 7  Bivariate Survey-Weighted Regression
text:
We use family = quasipoisson() rather than poisson(), because survey weights are not whole numbers. The estimates are the same.
A Poisson model’s own standard errors are wrong for a 0/1 outcome, but survey::svyglm() does not use them: it computes design-based (robust) standard errors from the weights, strata, and primary sampling units (PSUs).







TipWhy not odds ratios?



Logistic regression estimates odds ratios. When an outcome is common, as diabetes is (about one adult in eight), odds ratios are further from 1 than prevalence ratios and are easily misread as “times as likely”. Prevalence ratios mean what they say.

For each coefficient, Rubin’s rules combine the 5 results on the log scale (the estimate column above is already exponentiated into a PR):

the pooled estimate is the average of the 5 log PRs;
ubar is the average within-imputation variance (the usual squared standard error);
b is the between-imputation variance (how much the estimates differ across datasets);
t = ubar + (1 + 1/m) b is the total variance, which includes the uncertainty about the missing values;

8.3 Does income matter overall?
Income has four groups, so it has three PRs, each with its own p-value.   constraints = paste0("`", income_terms, "`"), # backticks: the names contain spaces
  method = "D1",

title: Appendix B — Reproducibility
text:
B.1 The same packages
Reproducing the survey chapters requires the same data, code, software, and settings. The steps below record those inputs and control the random-number streams.
R packages change between versions, and a new version can change a result. Open the project’s .Rproj file to activate renv, then restore the versions in renv.lock from the R console:
The lockfile records R 4.6.2 and the packages for every chapter. R and Quarto are installed separately. After intentional package changes, use renv::snapshot() to update the lockfile and renv::status() to check consistency. Python, if needed for additional scripts, has a separate uv environment; see the repository README.
The survey chapters need dplyr 1.2.0 or later, for dplyr::recode_values(). The session information at the end of this appendix lists the exact versions used to build the book. When you report results, report the versions you used.

section: B.2 The same random numbers: seeds
text:
B.2 The same random numbers: seeds
Multiple imputation draws random values. chapters/survey/_common.R sets the same seed (2024) at the start of every chapter. The imputation runs one task per imputation in parallel, and furrr::furrr_options(seed = seed) gives each task its own reproducible random-number stream, independent of the number of workers. This does not guarantee identical results after changes to data, software, or numerical libraries.

title: Appendix B — Reproducibility
text:
B.3 Smoke tests
A full render takes time because of the imputation. Before a full run, a smoke test checks that every survey chapter works:
quarto render chapters/survey --profile smoke
The smoke profile (_quarto-smoke.yml and _environment-smoke in the book’s root folder) sets the number of imputations to 2 and writes the book to _book-smoke/ and the data to data/brfss/processed-smoke/. Every page of a smoke book says “SMOKE TEST” in its title. The number of imputations is set in one place (N_IMPUTATIONS, read in _common.R), and every count in the code and text follows it.

title: Appendix B — Reproducibility
text:
B.4 Reusing expensive calculations
Expensive R chunks use #| cache: true, Quarto’s standard knitr cache. The setup records the chapter’s R code, contents of its input files, shared settings, R and package versions, and survey options in cache.extra. These inputs invalidate cached results when the analysis changes. Editing prose does not.
Full runs store their caches in data/brfss/processed/cache/; smoke runs use data/brfss/processed-smoke/cache/. Setup and file-saving chunks always run, so later chapters still receive their inputs on a cached render. Only rendering uses the cache; running individual lines in the R console executes them normally.
To recalculate all cached chunks in the survey chapters:
quarto render chapters/survey --cache-refresh
See the Quarto caching documentation for details. Validate the initial calculation before relying on cached results.

title: Appendix B — Reproducibility
section: B.5 Rendering the book without the data
text:
B.5 Rendering the book without the data
The survey chapters set freeze: auto (in chapters/survey/_metadata.yml). After someone renders them with the data, Quarto stores their results in _freeze/. When that folder is shared with the book, quarto render reuses the stored results, so the whole book renders on a computer without the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) files. Rendering the folder directly (quarto render chapters/survey) always re-runs the chapters.
